record.original_question: Can the methods used to count parking functions on random trees be extended to determine the total number of parking functions for other important labelled tree families, such as labelled binary trees and labelled ordered trees?

evidence.quote: (2) With the approach presented, one can also study the total number of parking functions for other important tree families as, e.g., labelled binary trees or labelled ordered trees.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $T$ be a rooted labelled tree on $n$ vertices, where the vertices serve as parking spaces and each edge is oriented toward the root (so each non-root vertex has a unique outgoing edge pointing to its parent). A parking function on $T$ is a sequence $(s_1,\dots,s_m)$ of vertices of $T$ (the preferred parking spots of $m$ drivers, $1\le m\le n$) defined by the following parking process: drivers arrive in order $1,2,\dots,m$; driver $i$ goes to vertex $s_i$ and, if it is empty, parks there; otherwise the driver moves along the directed edges toward the root, parking at the first empty vertex encountered. If the driver reaches the root and the root is occupied (or, more generally, leaves the tree without finding an empty vertex), the driver fails to park. The sequence $(s_1,\dots,s_m)$ is called a parking function (with $m$ successful drivers) if every driver succeeds in parking.

Two important families of size-$n$ rooted labelled trees are:
(a) labelled binary trees: rooted plane trees in which each vertex has at most two children, distinguished as left and right, with vertex labels forming a permutation of $\{1,\dots,n\}$;
(b) labelled ordered trees: rooted plane trees with an arbitrary number of linearly ordered children at each vertex, with vertex labels forming a permutation of $\{1,\dots,n\}$.

Let $F_n$ denote, for each family, the total number of pairs $(T,(s_1,\dots,s_n))$ where $T$ is a tree of size $n$ in the family and $(s_1,\dots,s_n)$ is a parking function on $T$ in which all $n$ drivers park successfully.

Problem. Determine, for each of the two families above, an exact formula and the asymptotic behaviour as $n\to\infty$ of $F_n$, by means of a generating-function or combinatorial-decomposition approach analogous to the one used for uniformly random labelled (Cayley) trees.
artifact.status_search_result: Enumeration of parking functions for labelled ordered, labelled unordered, and labelled binary tree families has been carried out by Kuba and Panholzer (e.g., "Parking functions for trees and mappings", arXiv:1504.04972, and a follow-up combinatorial-approach paper), yielding generating-function characterizations together with exact and asymptotic counts for trees of size n with n successful drivers. Thus the program of extending the methods to binary and ordered labelled trees has been substantially carried out, though related variants (e.g., parking on random binary trees, arXiv:2411.10296) continue to be studied.

status_evidence.title: Parking functions for trees and mappings
status_evidence.snippet: Enumeration problem for different kinds of tree parking functions for rooted labeled trees of important combinatorial tree families, including labeled ordered, unordered and binary trees.
status_evidence.claim: Total numbers of parking functions for labelled ordered, unordered, and binary trees have been determined via generating-function decompositions, with exact and asymptotic enumeration results.

status_evidence.title: A combinatorial approach for discrete car parking on random labelled trees
status_evidence.snippet: Combinatorial approach for parking on random labelled trees.
status_evidence.claim: A combinatorial decomposition approach has been applied to parking on labelled tree families.

status_evidence.title: Parking on a random rooted binary tree
status_evidence.snippet: Parking process on random binary trees.
status_evidence.claim: Parking on binary trees continues to be an active topic, indicating ongoing extensions and refinements.
